newsitem.title: INDIA: India party votes as split looms, but PM is safe.
newsitem.headline: India party votes as split looms, but PM is safe.

text.p: Leaders of Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's fractious Janata Dal party voted on Thursday to choose a president and struggled to seek peace with with its incumbent chief, who signalled an impending split in the party's ranks.
Despite the tensions, Laloo Prasad Yadav, the party's current president, gave assurances that his followers would continue to support Gujral's centre-left coalition.
Leaders of the Janata Dal, the largest group in Gujral's 15-party United Front, used the ballot box for the first time in the party's nine- year history to select their leaders.

The dose of democracy, imposed by an activist Election Commission and supported by India's Supreme Court, was obscured by a call by Yadav for his followers to boycott the voting. He alleged that the party's voter lists had been rigged against him.
Results of the balloting were not expected before Sunday.

Yadav, a low-caste leader and chief minister of the eastern state of Bihar, is said to command 16 Janata Dal lawmakers out of a total of 45. The ruling minority alliance, of which Janata Dal is part, has 178 members in the 545-seat lower house of parliament, the Lok Sabha.
A split in Janata Dal appeared increasingly certain. Yadav said his supporters would hold a convention in New Delhi on Saturday.
"Depending on the discussion and decision of the convention, we will decide our future course of action," Yadav said.
But he gave assurances that there was no threat to Gujral.
"My supporters will not pull down the Gujral government under any circumstance," he said. "We will under no circumstance allow him to be destablised."
The United News of India (UNI) news agency said Yadav's supporters were busy thinking up a name for the group.
"I don't think we will succeed (in stopping a split). I participated in voting because it is my duty," said a government minister and a Janata Dal leader who asked not to be identified.
"We are still trying, but hoping against hope," he said.
Yadav's troubles in the party coincided with a corruption scandal which has engulfed him and his party.
Yadav and 55 others have been indicted by federal police in a $280-million corruption case involving the alleged embezzlement of state animal husbandry funds.
Last month, the case forced a junior minister to resign from Gujral's two-month-old government. But Yadav, who says he is innocent, has refused to step down either as chief minister or party leader.

Gujral, who with other senior leaders has urged Yadav to quit, played down the split as he cast his vote at party headquarters in Delhi. "There could be differences of opinion and perception, but we all belong to one party," he said.
